claim: Cardiac glycosides (CGs) are highly toxic to animals because they are potent inhibitors of Na+,K+-ATPase (NKA).
source: CGs are highly toxic to animals because they are potent inhibitors of Na+,K+-ATPase (NKA), a ubiquitously expressed enzyme needed in a variety of cellular processes in animals, including neural signal transduction, muscle contraction, and osmoregulation (Lingrel, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lingrel, 2010, which provides external scholarly support for this statement.

claim: Mutations to NKA in invertebrates are typically homozygous lethal and associated with defects in locomotion, neuron development and neural homeostasis.
source: Mutations to NKA in invertebrates are typically homozygous lethal and associated with defects in locomotion, neuron development and neural homeostasis (Ashmore et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ashmore et al., 2009.

claim: In humans, loss-of-function mutations in NKA have been associated with several rare disorders such as dystonia, parkinsonism and hemiplegic migraines.
source: In humans, loss-of-function mutations in NKA have been associated with several rare disorders such as dystonia, parkinsonism and hemiplegic migraines (Bøttger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bøttger et al., 2012.

claim: NKAs have long been targeted with CG-based drugs to treat common conditions such as congestive heart failure and cardiac arrhythmias.
source: Despite their toxicity, NKAs have long been targeted with CG-based drugs to treat common conditions such as congestive heart failure and cardiac arrhythmias (Schoner, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schoner, 2002.

claim: In most CG-adapted insects, diet specialization on CG-containing hostplants has been accompanied by recurrent adaptive amino acid substitutions to the CG-binding domain of the alpha-subunit of NKA, ATPα1.
source: Indeed, in most cases, diet specialization on CG-containing hostplants has been accompanied by recurrent adaptive amino acid substitutions to the CG-binding domain of the alpha-subunit of NKA, ATPα1 (Zhen et al., 2012; Dobler et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhen et al., 2012; Dobler et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Previous studies have identified up to 35 sites in ATPα1 at which substitutions could contribute to CG-insensitivity.
source: Previous studies have identified up to 35 sites in ATPα1 at which substitutions could contribute to CG-insensitivity (reviewed in Zhen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Zhen et al., 2012.

claim: CG-insensitivity of ATPα1 most often arises via a highly similar pattern of substitution at two sites (111 and 122).
source: However, CG-insensitivity of ATPα1 most often arises via a highly similar pattern of substitution at two sites (111 and 122, Figure 1A): as an illustration, a survey of 28 CG-adapted insects revealed that 30 of 63 amino acid substitutions observed at sites implicated in CG-sensitivity in ATPα1 occur at sites 111 and 122 (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Yang et al., 2019 showing that 30 of 63 substitutions occur at sites 111 and 122.

claim: Sites 111 and 122 have been identified as targets of positive selection in CG-adapted insects using statistical phylogenetic methods.
source: Sites 111 and 122 have also been identified as targets of positive selection in CG-adapted insects using statistical phylogenetic methods (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Each of the nine engineered substitution lines exhibit severely reduced fitness, behaving effectively as recessive lethals.
source: To our surprise, however, each of the nine lines exhibit severely reduced fitness, behaving effectively as recessive lethals.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing reduced viability.

claim: Survivorship of individuals to adulthood is close to zero for all engineered substitution lines.
source: Nonetheless, survivorship of individuals to adulthood is close to zero for all lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: D. subobscura carries haplotypes resembling those engineered into D. melanogaster, including the ancestral (QN) and derived states (QH and VH) at sites 111 and 122, and yet are viable.
source: An important clue is provided by the observation that D. subobscura, a European relative of D. melanogaster, carries haplotypes resembling those that we engineered into D. melanogaster, including the ancestral (QN) and derived states (QH and VH) at sites 111 and 122, respectively (Pegueroles et al., 2016), and yet are viable.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pegueroles et al., 2016.

claim: PAML ancestral sequence reconstruction reveals that 21 amino acid substitutions distinguish the D. melanogaster ATPα1 from the ancestral D. subobscura protein.
source: PAML ancestral sequence reconstruction applied to full length coding sequences for D. subobscura (Materials and methods) and the closely related sister species D. guanche (Puerma et al., 2018) reveals that 21 amino acid substitutions distinguish the D. melanogaster ATPα1 from the ancestral D. subobscura protein.
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis using PAML and data from Puerma et al., 2018.

claim: Site 119 is among those having the strongest phylogenetic correlations with both sites 111 and 122 (top 5% of 270 sites).
source: Of the divergent sites between D. melanogaster and D. subobscura, only one site (119) is among those having the strongest phylogenetic correlations with both sites 111 and 122 (top 5% of 270 sites) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic correlation analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A substitution at 119 is observed in 90% of the cases in which there is a substitution at 111 and 100% of the cases in which there is a substitution at site 122.
source: A substitution at 119 is observed in 90% of the cases in which there is a substitution at 111 and 100% of the cases in which there is a substitution at site 122.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the multiple sequence alignment data.

claim: Site 119 was previously identified as one of four sites in the protein that underlie a CG-association/dissociation rate difference distinguishing human ATP1A1 and ATP1A2 isoforms.
source: Though site 119 is not among sites known to affect CG-sensitivity (Zhen et al., 2012), previous work identified it as one of four sites in the protein that underlie a CG-association/dissociation rate difference distinguishing human ATP1A1 and ATP1A2 isoforms (Crambert et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhen et al., 2012 and Crambert et al., 2004.

claim: A119S rescues the lethality associated with homozygosity for all four substitutions with which it was paired (Q111L, Q111V, Q111T, and N122H).
source: Remarkably, we find that A119S rescues the lethality associated with homozygosity for all four substitutions with which we paired it (i.e. compare Figure 1D with Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability data comparing Figure 1D with Figure 1B.

claim: Embryos homozygous for A119S, with and without substitutions at 111 and 122, have levels of hatchability and survival that are close to wild-type levels.
source: Embryos homozygous for A119S, with and without substitutions at 111 and 122, have levels of hatchability and survival that are close to wild-type levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The inhibition curve for A119S/+ appears to be monophasic.
source: With these considerations in mind, we note that the inhibition curve for A119S/+ appears to be monophasic (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on enzyme inhibition assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A119S alone likely encodes a functional enzyme that has little effect on CG inhibition of NKA.
source: Since A119S homozygotes are viable, we conclude that A119S alone likely encodes a functional enzyme that has little effect on CG inhibition of NKA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from viability data and enzyme inhibition curves.

claim: The inhibition curve for N122H/+ heterozygotes is biphasic (f = 0.18, 95% CI 0.14–0.24).
source: In contrast, the inhibition curve for N122H/+ heterozygotes is biphasic (f = 0.18, 95% CI 0.14–0.24).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data.

claim: N122H substantially increases CG-insensitivity (IC50,2 = 6.6e-6).
source: However, while this implies that N122H substantially increases CG-insensitivity (IC50,2 = 6.6e-6), the contribution of the N122H form to the total CG-inhibitable activity in heterozygotes (f) is estimated to be less than half that of the wild-type form.
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data.

claim: N122H+A119S/+ heterozygotes produce a strongly biphasic inhibition curve, with a two-fold higher estimated IC50,2 = 1.9e-5 and comparable levels of activity to that of the wild-type form (f = 0.53, 95% CI 0.47–0.56).
source: In contrast to N122H/+, N122H+A119S/+ heterozygotes produce a strongly biphasic inhibition curve, with a two-fold higher estimated IC50,2 = 1.9e-5 and comparable levels of activity to that of the wild-type form (f = 0.53, 95% CI 0.47–0.56, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The level of CG-insensitivity conferred by Q111L, Q111V, Q111T and N122H, in the presence of A119S, is estimated to be 7, 11, 28 and 178-fold greater than the wild-type form of the enzyme, respectively.
source: We estimate the level of CG-insensitivity conferred by Q111L, Q111V, Q111T and N122H, in the presence of A119S, to be 7, 11, 28 and 178-fold greater than the wild-type form of the enzyme, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All of the substitutions engineered at sites 111 and 122, individually and in combination, exhibit dominant bang sensitivity phenotypes that are similar in severity to those of the loss-of-function deletion Δ2-6b.
source: Examining our panel of substitutions for these effects reveals all of the substitutions we engineered at sites 111 and 122, individually and in combination, exhibit dominant bang sensitivity phenotypes that are similar in severity to those of the loss-of-function deletion Δ2-6b (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bang sensitivity phenotypes were indistinguishable from wild-type for all heterozygous substitutions at 111 and 122 in combination with A119S.
source: In contrast, bang sensitivity phenotypes were indistinguishable from wild-type for all heterozygous substitutions at 111 and 122 in combination with A119S (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Individuals homozygous for A119S, and substitutions at 111 and 122 in the presence of A119S, still exhibit obvious neural dysfunction relative to the wildtype.
source: Interestingly, individuals homozygous for A119S, and substitutions at 111 and 122 in the presence of A119S, still exhibit obvious neural dysfunction relative to the wildtype (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lines carrying substitutions at sites 111 and 122 in combination with A119S are all substantially less-sensitive to CG exposure than the wild-type strain.
source: While the wild-type strain suffers high levels of mortality upon CG exposure, the lines carrying substitutions at sites 111 and 122 in combination with A119S are all substantially less-sensitive (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by CG exposure assay data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The survival probability of A119S+N122H (SH/+ and SH/SH) is indistinguishable from control treatments in exposures with up to 10 mM ouabain.
source: Notably, the survival probability of A119S+N122H (SH/+ and SH/SH) is indistinguishable from control treatments in exposures with up to 10 mM ouabain.
evidence: The claim is supported by CG exposure assay data.

claim: A119S alone confers a substantial measure of insensitivity to CG-exposure (S/+ and S/S exhibit ~8.5 fold and ~21 fold lower relative risk, respectively, than wild-type at 5 mM ouabain).
source: First, a substantial measure of insensitivity to CG-exposure is also conferred by A119S alone (S/+ and S/S exhibit ~8.5 fold and ~21 fold lower relative risk, respectively, than wild-type at 5 mM ouabain, Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by CG exposure assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A119S alone has only a small effect on NKA sensitivity to CG-inhibition.
source: Despite this, A119S alone has only a small effect on NKA sensitivity to CG-inhibition (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Insensitivity to CG exposure is a partially dominant phenotype.
source: Further, the substantially improved survival of heterozygous strains relative to the wild-type strain, including to some extent A119S/+, suggests that insensitivity to CG exposure is a partially dominant phenotype (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from CG exposure assay data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Despite the lethal homozygous effects of Q111V and N122H individually, the dominant effects of these substitutions on insensitivity to CG-exposure imply that they have the potential to confer a fitness advantage as heterozygotes in CG-rich environments.
source: Importantly, despite the lethal homozygous effects of Q111V and N122H individually (Figure 1B), the dominant effects of these substitutions on insensitivity to CG-exposure imply that they have the potential to confer a fitness advantage as heterozygotes in CG-rich environments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from viability and CG exposure data.

claim: Adaptive substitutions conferring CG-insensitivity at sites 111 and 122 most often arise on a genetic background that includes a substitution at site 119.
source: As we show, with few exceptions, adaptive substitutions conferring CG-insensitivity at sites 111 and 122 most often arise on a genetic background that includes a substitution at site 119, a site not previously implicated in CG-sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and experimental data.

claim: The most commonly observed substitution at site 119, A119S, rescues the lethality and dominant effects on neural function associated with substitutions at sites 111 and 122 in D. melanogaster.
source: We further show that the most commonly observed substitution at site 119, A119S, rescues the lethality and dominant effects on neural function associated with substitutions at sites 111 and 122 in D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability and bang sensitivity assay data.

claim: A second common substitution, A119N, appears independently in three insect orders and may act similarly to A119S.
source: A second common substitution, A119N, appears independently in three insect orders and may act similarly (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic patterns shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1, with speculation about functional similarity.

claim: Many of the amino acid substitutions associated with CG-adaptation (i.e. Q111L, Q111E, Q111H, A119S, and N122H) can all be reached by single nucleotide substitutions.
source: It is notable that many of the amino acid substitutions associated with CG-adaptation (i.e. Q111L, Q111E, Q111H, A119S, and N122H), can all be reached by single nucleotide substitutions, whereas others (e.g. Q111V, Q111T) require two nucleotide substitutions.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the genetic code and mutational pathways.

claim: Q111V can be reached by single substitutions via intermediates Q111L and Q111E, both of which are observed among multiple CG-adapted insects.
source: Q111V can be reached by single substitutions via intermediates Q111L and Q111E, both of which are observed among multiple CG-adapted insects (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of mutational pathways and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Q111T, which has arisen independently at least three times across insect orders, requires passing through states Q111P or Q111K via single nucleotide substitutions, but neither are observed among the taxa surveyed.
source: In contrast, Q111T, which has arisen independently at least three times across insect orders, require passing through states Q111P or Q111K via single nucleotide substitutions, but neither are observed among the taxa surveyed (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of mutational pathways and phylogenetic data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The lack of observed instances of Q111P or Q111K suggests that these states may be particularly deleterious and are either evolutionarily short-lived or circumvented altogether by dinucleotide mutation events.
source: The lack of observed instances of Q111P or Q111K suggests that these states may be particularly deleterious and are either evolutionarily short-lived or circumvented altogether by dinucleotide mutation events.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from phylogenetic patterns and speculation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Mutinucleotide mutation events are more frequent than previously appreciated.
source: The latter scenario is made more plausible by recent work in Drosophila indicating that mutinucleotide mutation events are more frequent than previously appreciated (Assaf et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Assaf et al., 2017.

claim: To the extent that D. melanogaster represents a typical CG-sensitive species, substitutions at positions 111 and 122 would not be permitted to fix in the species without being preceded by A119S or an equivalent permissive substitution.
source: To the extent that D. melanogaster represents a typical CG-sensitive species, it is clear that substitutions at positions 111 and 122 would not be permitted to fix in the species without being preceded by A119S or an equivalent permissive substitution.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results showing lethality of 111/122 substitutions without A119S.

claim: A119S was not detected in extensive mutagenesis screens.
source: A119S was not detected in extensive mutagenesis screens (Zhen et al., 2012) and has only modest effects on CG-inhibition of NKA in vitro (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhen et al., 2012 and enzyme inhibition data in Figure 2.

claim: Homozygosity for A119S results in substantial levels of neural dysfunction.
source: In particular, we show that homozygosity for A119S results in substantial levels of neural dysfunction (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A119S, even when heterozygous, confers a substantial survival advantage upon exposure to CGs.
source: Despite these detrimental effects, we also find that A119S, even when heterozygous, confers a substantial survival advantage upon exposure to CGs.
evidence: The claim is supported by CG exposure assay data.

claim: In multiple lineages, the substitutions A119S and A119N preceded substitutions to 111 and 122 (Hemiptera, Hymenoptera, Diptera).
source: In multiple lineages, the substitutions A119S and A119N preceded substitutions to 111 and 122 (Hemiptera, Hymenoptera, Diptera).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: In Drosophila, A119S was established before substitutions to sites 111 and 122 in the evolutionary lineage leading to D. subobscura, which appears to be polymorphic with respect to CG-insensitivity.
source: In Drosophila, where we have the greatest phylogenetic resolution, A119S was established before substitutions to sites 111 and 122 in the evolutionary lineage leading to D. subobscura, which appears to be polymorphic with respect to CG-insensitivity.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis and inference.

claim: Q111L is sometimes observed in the absence of A119S (as is Q111E), implying alternative permissive substitutions in these taxa.
source: This said, Q111L is sometimes observed in the absence of A119S (as is Q111E, see Figure 1A: Bemisa tabaci and Lophocarya caryae; not shown are Aedes aegypti, Mechanitis polymia and Empyreuma pugione, see Supplementary file 1) implying alternative permissive substitutions in these taxa.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1, with inference about alternative mechanisms.

claim: A119S is a common substitution among taxa that do not specialize on CG-containing hostplants, implying the existence of additional compensatory substitutions in these species.
source: More generally, A119S is a common substitution among taxa that do not specialize on CG-containing hostplants (Supplementary file 1), again implying the existence of additional compensatory substitutions in these species.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic data in Supplementary file 1 and inference about compensatory mechanisms.

claim: CG-insensitive haplotypes including A119S lack strong deleterious effects and may confer a survival advantage upon exposure to CGs when heterozygous.
source: Alternatively, since CG-insensitive haplotypes substitutions including A119S lack strong deleterious effects and may confer a survival advantage upon exposure to CGs when heterozygous (Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), such haplotypes may be maintained over time by heterozygote advantage and subsequently reach fixation as they accumulate a sufficient number of compensatory substitutions (Kimura, 1985) or by gene duplication (Spofford, 1969), which has occurred repeatedly in CG-specialist species (Zhen et al., 2012; Petschenka et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4, with speculation about evolutionary mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: D. subobscura is polymorphic for substitutions at positions 111 and 122 mediating CG-insensitivity and these haplotypes are associated with polymorphic inversions that may rarely be homozygous.
source: Interestingly, D. subobscura is polymorphic for substitutions at positions 111 and 122 mediating CG-insensitivity and these haplotypes are associated with polymorphic inversions that may rarely be homozygous (Pegueroles et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pegueroles et al., 2016.

claim: The evolution of CG-insensitivity in D. subobscura may be recent and represent a transient stage in the evolution of this adaptive trait.
source: The evolution of CG-insensitivity in D. subobscura may be recent and represent a transient stage in the evolution of this adaptive trait.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the polymorphic state observed in D. subobscura.

claim: Protein dysfunction associated with CG-insensitivity substitutions may be compensated by the up-regulation of ATPα1 expression.
source: Another alternative is that protein dysfunction associated with CG-insensitivity substitutions is in some cases compensated by the up-regulation of ATPα1 expression (see for e.g. Loehlin et al., 2019), which may be an important driver of recurrent ATPα1 duplication and is observed across multiple CG-adapted insects (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by citations to Loehlin et al., 2019 and Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Dominance and epistasis of amino acid substitutions can be missed or mischaracterized in the absence of a whole animal model to evaluate these effects.
source: By considering phenotypic effects both in vitro and in vivo, we demonstrate how dominance and epistasis of amino acid substitutions can be missed or mischaracterized in the absence of a whole animal model to evaluate these effects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo results presented in the study.

claim: Multiple insect species specializing on CG-containing host-plants have independently duplicated and neofunctionalized ATPα1.
source: Support for this hypothesis comes from the fact that multiple insect species specializing on CG-containing host-plants have independently duplicated and neofunctionalized ATPα1.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: In all cases examined to date, species with two or more copies of ATPα1 retain one minimally altered copy that is more highly expressed in nervous tissue, and have evolved one or more insensitive copies that are more highly expressed in the gut.
source: In all cases examined to date, species with two or more copies retain one minimally altered copy that is more highly expressed in nervous tissue, and have evolved one or more insensitive copies that are more highly expressed in the gut, the site of absorption of CGs (Zhen et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhen et al., 2012 and Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of engineered ATPα1 constructs in cell lines suggests that some duplicate-specific CG-insensitivity substitutions appear to reduce NKA activity.
source: Further support for negative pleiotropic effects is provided by the expression of engineered ATPα1 constructs in cell lines, suggesting that some duplicate-specific CG-insensitivity substitutions appear to reduce NKA activity (Dalla and Dobler, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dalla and Dobler, 2016.

claim: Flies heterozygous for loss-of-function ATPα1 substitutions have significantly longer recovery times than wild-type flies.
source: Flies heterozygous for loss-of-function ATPα1 substitutions are known to have significantly longer recovery times than wild-type flies (see for e.g. Δ2-6b/+ relative to +/+ in panel A, p=4.5e-7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing significant differences in recovery times.

claim: The recovery-time distributions for S/+, VS/+ and SH/+ are indistinguishable from the engineered wild-type strain (+/+).
source: The recovery-time distributions for S/+, VS/+ and SH/+ are indistinguishable from the engineered wild-type strain (+/+).
evidence: The claim is supported by bang sensitivity assay data.

claim: Recovery times are significantly longer than wild-type for lines with individual substitutions V/+ and H/+ (p=1.3e-5 and p=5.2e-4, respectively) and are indistinguishable from the loss-of-function deletion mutation Δ2-6b/+.
source: In contrast, recovery times are significantly longer than wild-type for lines with individual substitutions V/+ and H/+ (p=1.3e-5 and p=5.2e-4, respectively) and are indistinguishable from the loss-of-function deletion mutation Δ2-6b/+.
evidence: The claim is supported by bang sensitivity assay data with statistical significance values.

claim: Recovery times for homozygous lines S/S, VS/VS and SH/SH are all significantly longer than for heterozygotes S/+, VS/+, and SH/+ (p<3.3e-3).
source: Recovery times for homozygous lines S/S, VS/VS and SH/SH are all significantly longer than for heterozygotes S/+, VS/+, and SH/+ (p<3.3e-3).
evidence: The claim is supported by bang sensitivity assay data with statistical significance values.

claim: A119S ameliorates the dominant dysfunction caused by Q111V and N122H but residual recessive neural dysfunction is still apparent in homozygotes that include A119S.
source: These results demonstrate epistasis between substitutions at sites 119 and 111/122 at the level of neural function. A119 ameliorates the dominant dysfunction caused by Q111V and N122H but residual recessive neural dysfunction is still apparent in homozygotes that include A119S.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from bang sensitivity assay data comparing heterozygotes and homozygotes.
